title: Stock up on food to prepare for extreme El Niño weather, minister says
description: Households should stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean, a go
body: Households should stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean, a government minister has said.Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle told the Guardian the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country".Her comments came as the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis.The NAO said the government was too reliant on the private sector to deal with food supply disruption. The government is due to unveil a strategy about preparing for national emergencies later this year.Dame Angela said, external: "We're about to experience probably the largest El Niño that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country."It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously."If you've got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you're going to be a lot better off than if you haven't."So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient."Her comments came as an NAO report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.It also cited climate change as a longer-term chronic risk which could leave Britain's food supply at risk.The disruptions could push up prices and leave vulnerable people struggling to buy food, it said.The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) was too reliant on private companies to handle disruptions to food supply. It added the department had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland, Sweden and European Union nations, the NAO added.It said ministers should encourage households to prepare for supply chain disruptions and learn from the approaches taken by other countries.Defra said the report showed food supply risks were becoming more complex and the government was working with farmers and industry to strengthen the UK's resilience."While our food businesses and supermarkets have continued to feed the nation through significant disruption, we will carefully consider the report's findings and recommendations as part of our ongoing work to build a more resilient, productive and sustainable food system," a spokesperson said.In July, the government announced plans to set out the "small but important steps" households can take to prepare for food and water shortages in the event of extreme weather or cyber-attacks. These will form a strategy to be unveiled by the end of 2026 aimed at bringing the UK closer into line with European countries in terms of emergency preparedness. Phil Pluck, chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, the body which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, said Britain was "pretty close to crisis".He told the BBC's Wake Up to Money programme that the country was being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system".He added that El Niño, as well as global shipping disruption and the threat of pandemics, mean you cannot "just rely on the private sector coming through every single time".Asked whether people should be stocking up in case of disruptions, Pluck added: "Yes, we should."There should be some sensible stocking in each household. And the government in the autumn will be telling all of us to do that."

schema.headline: Stock up on food to prepare for extreme El Niño weather, minister says

title: Russian drone hits Ukranian security headquarters, Zelensky says
description: "All emergency services are on the scene. Everyone affected will receive the necessary assistance," Zelensky added in a message on Telegram."I instruc
body: "All emergency services are on the scene. Everyone affected will receive the necessary assistance," Zelensky added in a message on Telegram."I instructed Poklad to deliver an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike, to the Russians once everything is ready. Our military will support this response."Images of the office widely shared online showed black smoke pouring from two windows on the front of the building.Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said the attack was a "major escalation that demands resolute responses"."Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace - laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy," he added.Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people had been hurt in the SBU attack, but did not elaborate on whether they were inside the offices.A nearby café was damaged and one customer was taken to hospital after the strike.Stanislav Zavertaylo, co-owner of the popular Zavertailo chain, told the BBC that this was his third café to have been damaged since the start of the full-scale invasion."Now I'm in shock because there's a lot of damage. All the windows are broken, there's a lot of glass, garbage" he added.The Russian defence ministry also said on Friday it had struck a cargo vessel in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk and a tanker near Odesa.In recent weeks Russia has escalated its daytime strikes on Ukrainian targets.In many instances it has employed jet-powered drones which are faster and harder to intercept. It is not yet known which type of munition was used in this latest attack.

schema.headline: Russian drone hits Ukranian security headquarters, Zelensky says

title: Xbox to limit cloud gaming to 15 hours a month for Game Pass users
description: Xbox is introducing strict monthly time limits for Game Pass subscribers who stream games online through its cloud gaming service.The changes, which c
body: Xbox is introducing strict monthly time limits for Game Pass subscribers who stream games online through its cloud gaming service.The changes, which come into effect in November, will see a subscriber to the  £16.99 Ultimate monthly plan able to stream games for up to 15 hours a month - before having to purchase additional cloud play time.Xbox said the limits were due to the rising cost of cloud gaming, and they would allow the firm to "continue to invest" in the service's "reliability and performance". While some questioned, external whether the service was used by many to begin with, others called out, external the additional limits for subscribers.Cloud gaming allows players to stream and play games online from a remote server using a phone, tablet or controller, rather than downloading and running it on a PC or console at home.Different tiers of subscription to Game Pass will have different limits.Premium users will get 10 hours, while those on the basic Essential tier will get five hours a month before they have to pay for extra time.Xbox claimed just 4% of the people who use Games Pass - its Netflix-style subscription plan for games - use its cloud gaming service.A recent Wall Street Journal article, external reported Game Pass has 30 million subscribers, which would leave the number of people affected by the cloud gaming changes at roughly 1.2 million."This is a pretty awful change, hopefully Xbox adds an extra zero on the end cause 15hrs is abysmal. 30 minutes a day, really?" posted one commenter on X, external.Jez Corden of Windows Central told the BBC the announcement showed that "absolutely nothing is safe from the AI-driven component crisis," but he added it also highlighted "where Microsoft's priorities are".Both cloud gaming and AI use data centres to process information."For them to continue to offer unlimited access to Microsoft Copilot [AI] for free but restrict paid cloud gaming in this way shows some contradiction," he added.Xbox said in a blog post, external that from November, users would also be able to use the company's cloud gaming feature without subscribing to Game Pass, but by buying "cloud playtime hours" through the Xbox store.It has not revealed how much extra hours of cloud gaming would cost.The news comes as Asha Sharma, Xbox's chief executive, told the BBC in an exclusive recent interview that the company and the industry as a whole needed to "start to innovate on affordability and efficiency," amid a "crisis" in computing prices."As an industry, we're in the middle of 'Rampocalypse'. We're in the middle of people coming back from Covid and the patterns changing," she said."Rampocalypse" refers to the fact that the cost of a previously cheap hardware component, random access memory (Ram), has shot up in price with the expansion of compute-hungry data centres. Some people also call it "Ramageddon".Sharma added: "Within Xbox, we haven't been healthy. And so a lot of the reset that will take us throughout the year is really meant to help ensure that we are here for the next 25 years and we're continuing to serve our purpose and our mission."According to Xbox owner Microsoft's July financial filings, external, annual Xbox revenue dropped by $1.7bn to roughly $21.8bn (£16.1bn) - a 7% decline from 2025.Part of Sharma's reset has seen 3,200 people let go at the company - with 1,600 job losses announced in July, and the remaining posts to go gradually over the course of Microsoft's 2027 financial year.Studios which had been acquired by Xbox - including Compulsion Games, which made the Bafta-winning South of Midnight and Double Fine Productions, makers of Psychonauts - were also made independent again.Sharma is betting these changes can reverse its fortunes despite concerns over its subscription strategy and rising AI-related costs."Sometimes you have to restructure a business when it's not doing well, and that was true with our Xbox business," Microsoft's president Brad Smith recently told the BBC.

schema.headline: Xbox to limit cloud gaming to 15 hours a month for Game Pass users

title: Lindsay Clancy's case ended in a mistrial - what happens next?
description: Figure caption, Watch moment judge in Clancy case says a mistrial likelyByMadeline Halpert and Sareen HabeshianUpdated 7 minutes agoAfter a week of mu
body: Figure caption, Watch moment judge in Clancy case says a mistrial likelyByMadeline Halpert and Sareen HabeshianUpdated 7 minutes agoAfter a week of mulling Lindsay Clancy's fate, a judge has declared a mistrial in the case of the US mother accused of murdering her three young children.It came after the jury said they could not reach a unanimous verdict on whether Clancy was guilty of murder.The declaration opens the door to a host of possibilities about what happens next.Clancy, who faced three counts of first-degree murder, does not deny killing her children in 2023 but pleaded not guilty, with her lawyers arguing she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible. The prosecution said she made a calculated, intentional decision to kill them.What is a mistrial? Under US law, the jury must unanimously reach a conclusion "beyond a reasonable doubt". If they cannot, the judge can call a mistrial, which ends the trial with no verdict.Jurors in Clancy's trial had been deadlocked for days, and told the judge three times that they were unable to come to a unanimous decision.Sullivan, who is overseeing the trial, previously urged them to continue deliberating until there is no possible chance of a decision. In a last-ditch effort he issued additional instructions, known as a Tuey-Rodriguez charge in the state, encouraging the panel to consider all perspectives and ensuring jurors were questioning and examining their own views in the case. The jury continued to indicate they could not come to a consensus, leading the judge to say he had no choice but to declare a mistrial.This does not mean prosecutors have proven their case, nor does it mean the defendant is not guilty.Now, the prosecution could either refile and restart with a new jury or negotiate a plea agreement. Alternatively, prosecutors could dismiss the charges altogether.Figure caption, Watch: BBC's Ione Wells explains how the Lindsay Clancy trial could endWill Lindsay Clancy go free?Not immediately. Clancy will remain held under the same murder charges in the mental health facility where she is currently housed as lawyers weigh their next steps.If a new trial is planned, Clancy will remain in that facility until it begins - though her lawyers could ask for a review of her bail situation, said Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and expert in mental health law.Even as a new trial is being prepared, prosecutors could still negotiate with Clancy's team over a plea agreement, Cucolo said.Will prosecutors ask for a new trial?In serious felony cases like these, prosecutors often ask for a retrial. If they do, the jury selection process will take place once again and a new trial will be scheduled with a new set of jurors.The time it could take to schedule another trial will depend on factors including the court schedule, any legal requests either side may file, and how long it may take to line up expert witnesses. The six-week trial in Massachusetts captured significant public interest, with crowds sometimes gathering outside. "A case like this that obviously has been so high profile, and there is so much of an emotional response to this to the facts of this case, I think it's very likely that the prosecutor will ask for a retrial," Cucolo said.Image source, Patti Anne PhotographyImage caption, Clancy's children Cora (left), eight-month-old Callan (centre) and three-year-old DawsonWhy was the jury deadlocked?That is unclear, but it's been a complex case with each side presenting a huge amount of expert testimony.The identities of the nine women and three men on the jury has not been made public, and the judge banned any photographing or filming of them to retain their anonymity.But once the case is over, a juror can choose whether or not to speak publicly about the case and their deliberations.Following other high-profile trials, jurors have in some instances come forward to discuss the case, even writing books or doing media interviews.So while it remains unknown to the public what has gone on behind closed doors, more could be revealed in the coming days or weeks.If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide. www.befrienders.org.In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline

schema.headline: Lindsay Clancy's case ended in a mistrial - what happens next?

title: How could US-Iran conflict end? Three experts give their views
description: Jason Campbell, Senior Fellow at the Middle East Institute, Washington DCThe problem is we still do not know definitively what the US strategic object
body: Jason Campbell, Senior Fellow at the Middle East Institute, Washington DCThe problem is we still do not know definitively what the US strategic objectives are in Iran. The White House is persistently re-evaluating what it is willing to live with from a political standpoint.It was assumed the military component would be enough for a quick victory and that has not had the desired effect.What we are seeing is different levers - both military and economic - that the US is trying to pull at.Right now, the administration appears satisfied with some form of stasis. I think they are satisfied with maintaining the blockade and with allowing some periodic targeting against Iran's capability to upset the shipping lane in the strait.US officials are hopeful that the new sanctions will be enough to compel the Iranian regime to come to the negotiating table in a weaker position.US forces have seemingly been able to facilitate a sufficient trickle through the Strait of Hormuz in recent days to avert an oil-price shock or a global economic collapse. But those were not the US objectives when starting the war.My sense is that Iran is likely to demand a high price to get to a resolution, which is likely to remain politically untenable for the Trump administration.Dr Aniseh Bassiri Tabrizi, Associate Fellow with Chatham House's Middle East and North Africa Programme, LondonI do not think the latest strikes really alter Iranian calculations on the war. I think Tehran is preparing for an increased squeeze on its economy, and a continuation of the on and off attacks which we have seen over the past couple of months. Their intent will be to respond to these attacks in a proportionate manner in order not to spiral a larger conflict.On the economic side, obviously this is likely to hurt the Iranian economy which has already been affected by the war and has had underlying structural issues anyway, as we know from the December and January demonstrations in Iran.But I do not feel like there is the sense from the Iranian side that the economic squeeze is going to alter the Iranian calculation any time soon, including on any negotiations.That does not mean Iran is not looking for an off ramp, but I think what we are seeing is that it is waiting for the US to go back to the MoU, or to at least offer some sort of concession. Tehran does not want to cave in to US pressure or alter its own approach in response to sanctions or additional attacks.Nicholas Hopton, Distinguished Fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute think tank in London and former UK ambassador to IranThe latest spike in military action is not going to produce Iran's capitulation - it is just the latest twist. Economic pressure is also unlikely to work because China, Russia and many other countries which trade with Iran are not going to support unilateral US sanctions.Iran can continue to disrupt the Strait of Hormuz - they have a thumb on the jugular of the global economy.What is the White House's exit strategy? Well, the US has already found it. If Trump was able to put a sustained effort into negotiating the deal outlined in June's MoU, that is the off-ramp.Not only would a deal give the US a kind of victory because it would weaken the hardliners in the Islamic Republic, but also reassure everyone that Iran is not going to get a nuclear weapon.There is a silver bullet in the MoU which is the lifting of all US sanctions on Iran.What lifting those sanctions would do over time is weaken Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp (IRGC). Economic engagement between the outside world and Iran in a new way would gradually force radical political and social change - so you end up with an Islamic regime, but of a very different nature.Of course, that would not be straightforward to achieve, because of extensive IRGC penetration of the Iranian economy. But it should work, if given enough time and if the US and its partners exercised strategic patience which, sadly, is in short supply at this point.For the time being, I think we're going to carry on with a messy, inconclusive situation that is bad for everyone.

schema.headline: How could US-Iran conflict end? Three experts give their views

title: Health minister calls meeting on Wales transgender surgery pause
description: A meeting to discuss the decision to immediately pause referrals for gender-affirming surgeries in Wales has been called by the health minister.The We
body: A meeting to discuss the decision to immediately pause referrals for gender-affirming surgeries in Wales has been called by the health minister.The Welsh Gender Service paused surgery last week after concerns from an NHS committee about the number of referrals and whether they were all appropriate.Wales' health minister, Mabon ap Gwynfor, is meeting with members of the NHS Wales Joint Commissioning Committee (NWJCC), which instructed Cardiff and Vale University Health Board to halt both new referrals and planned surgeries, on Friday.The health board is responsible for the running of the NHS gender identity clinic which provides specialist care and support for adults in Wales.The decision was prompted by data which indicated "significantly higher rates of referral for gender affirming surgery... compared with English gender services" in 2025-26, according to the health board.The NWJCC has requested an independent clinical review be carried out, describing the move as "precautionary and clinically-led".First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth previously said the review into surgery services at must be quick.Plaid leader ap Iorwerth said while the committee at the heart of the row had taken the decision "for the right reason" on service quality grounds, he wanted a "resolution quickly".Cardiff and Vale University Health Board confirmed on Tuesday that some patients who had been awaiting gender-affirming surgery were already in hospital for their procedures when they were told of the suspension.Gender-affirming surgery encompasses both masculinising and feminising procedures, which often involve reshaping the genitalia. The procedures are irreversible.The Welsh Gender Service provides referrals for patients living in Wales, but all NHS surgeries are carried out in England.Reform UK and the Welsh Conservatives both welcomed the decision to pause surgeries.Ap Gwynfor said that, while he respected the decision was taken on the basis of clinical evidence, he had questions for the NWJCC."I want to understand how long this review will take, what form will it take and to make sure that people out there know that services are there and that they can depend on the NHS in Wales to help them out in their hour of need," he said.A letter, signed by 26 of Plaid Cymru's 28 backbench Senedd members, was sent to the chairman of the NWJCC, Ian Green, on Monday, expressing "profound disappointment" with the decision.The letter, which emerged on Thursday, added the development had "caused distress, fear and a deep sense of uncertainty" among the trans community, "at a time when the rights and dignity of trans people across the UK are increasingly under pressure".The group asked the NWJCC to set out what specifically had led to their cause for concern regarding the number of referrals and asked when surgeries and referrals would resume.Reform's Welsh leader, Dan Thomas, said that "sensible-minded people in Wales" would welcome the suspension, adding there was "more to do to ensure a comprehensive review of the service".Natasha Asghar, Welsh Conservative spokesperson for health, had earlier called for a review of the service.She said cancelling surgeries was "absolutely the right thing to do".

schema.headline: Health minister calls meeting on Wales transgender surgery pause

title: Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage and Russia is the chief suspect
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Germany said the attack at Leipzig airport was part of a pattern of "Russian hybrid operations" in EuropeBySarah R
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Germany said the attack at Leipzig airport was part of a pattern of "Russian hybrid operations" in EuropeBySarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondentUpdated 1 hour agoAs summer temperatures in Europe smashed records and many politicians shifted to holiday mode, Russia remained focused on its war.Not only did its military attacks across Ukraine intensify last month, becoming ever more deadly for civilians, Russia also appears to have escalated its sabotage campaign across Europe.This time, military and defence sector sites were the prime target.A full month after drones packed with explosives were found at Leipzig's airport, used by Ukraine to transport military goods, Germany's interior minister has declared that "Russia is responsible".Russia's President Vladimir Putin is demanding proof, as always, and his officials call the accusation "absurd".But the drones were just a dramatic start. August then brought a series of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia.Some of the affected countries have already blamed Russia; others are still investigating and some fires may eventually be ruled accidental, exactly as such attacks are designed to seem.Poland's interior minister is clear."There are many, many signals that Russia is changing its strategy and intensifying its activities, including terrorist and sabotage activities," Marcin Kierwiński said, warning people to be on their guard.August campaign across Europe4 August Germany: The first drone at Leipzig airport is discovered.10 August Bulgaria: A major fire breaks out at a warehouse of defence firm EMCO in Tryavna. In a statement, the company recalled previous blasts at its facilities which were investigated for links to Russia. "Human error is excluded," it said.13 August Italy: A fire at KNDS Ammo Italy outside Rome triggers a large explosion. The local prosecutor is looking into possible outside interference, La Repubblica newspaper reports. Publicly, his office will only confirm that a case has been opened for negligent disaster against "unknown persons".15 August Estonia: The Milrem Robotics factory in Tallinn, which the Kyiv Post says supplies drones to Ukraine, goes up in flames. Two suspects are arrested.Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal says the possibility of Russian sabotage is being "taking seriously" by investigators.25 August Slovakia: Police announce they have averted an arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer and seized a "large amount of incendiary mixture". The firm itself blames Russia and police arrest three suspects who they say were "following orders". Slovakia is Russia's close ally in Europe.30 August Poland: A country which is heavily targeted for sabotage reports two more fires. One is in Lublin at a company which produces helicopter components. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said arson "cannot be ruled out". An attack on the drone producer, WB Group, is clearer cut. A masked man is caught on CCTV throwing incendiary devices. Tusk calls it a "continuation of Russia's escalatory activities".The pattern has continued into September with two Bulgarians arrested in Munich, Germany, for suspected arson after throwing incendiary devices from a car at defence firm Rhode & Schwartz.Separately, police say they are hunting a climate extremist suspected of sabotage attacks this week on power substations in western Germany.Image source, EPAImage caption, The 31 August fire at Skarżysko-Kamienna targeted one of Poland's biggest defence firmsWhy is this happening now?Attacks on military and defence targets are not new, although previous acts of sabotage linked to Russia include more puzzling targets - such as an Ikea store and a Polish paint store.The novelty now is the concentration of cases."The intensity of military sites being attacked we've seen over the past couple of weeks is unusual," Daniela Richterova of the Department of War Studies at King's College says.She links the spike to developments in Russia's invasion of Ukraine."We've basically seen Ukraine take the war to Russia and strike deep inside Russian territory…They [Moscow] are under pressure, they have to do something."Whilst some sabotage is staged to sow chaos or fear, Richterova believes the Kremlin's aim right now is "coercive signalling": pressuring countries to stop supporting Kyiv by raising the stakes. After a slow start, Germany is Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid.There are other theories.To some, Russia is less concerned about "turning off the taps" of supplies to Ukraine and more about testing Nato for weaknesses."Russia is probing the boundaries of what's acceptable and collecting information on the results. They find out what works, and what's vulnerable," argues Keir Giles from the Chatham House think tank.He sees the sabotage campaign as preparation for the "next phase", as he puts it, of Russia's aggression in Europe."They're assessing the willingness of the victim country to actually do something about it."The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), which tracks sabotage cases, points to a previous surge in 2024 when Ukraine's allies began allowing it to use Western-supplied weapons deeper inside Russia.2024 was the year of the parcel bomb plot, when Russia was accused of sending packages containing liquid explosive to the UK and Poland. One ignited shortly before it was loaded on to a DHL cargo plane. It is thought this was a test run for something significantly bigger.Image source, Police handoutImage caption, Four parcels were sent from Lithuania to the UK and Poland in 2024 - two caught fire, at a warehouse in the UK and at Leipzig's airport"That was a marked high in terms of their willingness to inflict mass casualties," Giles adds.It was a step so serious, the White House contacted the Kremlin to tell it to stop. Russia had probed and found the limit.But the attacks have continued. German media on Friday quoted a federal police report that lists more than 165 suspected sabotage cases nationwide this year, though they don't say who is responsible.Who are the suspected saboteurs?Reports from Germany suggest the men who loaded and launched the drones at Leipzig's airport were Russian, and at least one may have entered the country specially for this job.That would be unusual.The vast majority of sabotage attacks in Europe have been carried out by Russian proxies: its so-called "gig economy saboteurs".They are usually Russian-speakers from former Soviet states, recruited online and driven by the cash, not political conviction.In one case the BBC reported from Poland, the saboteurs-for-hire had previously fought for Ukraine as volunteers.The "handlers" are generally thought to remain in Russia, co-ordinating operations online.The IISS likened the proxies they used to kamikaze drones: cheap and easy to launch in large numbers, but disposable.The amateurs can be sloppy or reckless, though. In the parcel plot, one man failed to find a pick-up point and the whole mission had to be aborted.So if Moscow did send professionals for the Leipzig drone launch, it suggests it wanted precision - and success.In fact, the devices appear to have malfunctioned.Nato faced with Soviet-style campaignRussia's sabotage operations seem to come from the Cold War playbook. Daniela Richterova's research shows very similar targets on Soviet sabotage lists, and agents-saboteurs were used in much the same way.The idea, she says, was to have small, deniable attacks in peace-time that would escalate in times of war."I think we are still in the grey zone between the two, but the kind of attacks we've seen in the past weeks shrink that zone," she says. "And I think that increases the risk of what happens next."As Nato scrambles to respond, questions like how many small, individual attacks add up to a sustained Russian assault - and demand action - remain unanswered.Perhaps riskier than all is the potential for escalation by accident.What if the exploding parcel had gone off mid-air and caused a crash? What if the Leipzig drone had brought down a plane?"I think it could result in a big attack," Richterova says. "Then Nato, in this heightened security environment, would not be able to ignore that, and have to react."

schema.headline: Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage and Russia is the chief suspect

title: US Open 2026 results: Aryna Sabalenka's win over Kamilla Rakhimova interrupted by cannabis smell
description: Aryna Sabalenka briefly halted her US Open match against Kamilla Rakhimova because of a strong smell of cannabis before cruising into the fourth round
body: Aryna Sabalenka briefly halted her US Open match against Kamilla Rakhimova because of a strong smell of cannabis before cruising into the fourth round in New York.Top seed Sabalenka raised the issue after going 3-0 up in the first set against Uzbekistan's Rakhimova, telling umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore that "someone is smoking weed".The Belarusian asked the umpire to intervene "because it's so strong".Asderaki-Moore spoke to an official on her radio and made a smoking gesture to someone behind her, before play continued.Two-time defending champion Sabalenka went on to secure a confident 6-3 6-4 victory on Louis Armstrong Stadium as she chases a fifth Grand Slam singles title.Sabalenka is not the first player at this year's US Open to complain about smelling cannabis on court at Flushing Meadows.Last week, Britain's Katie Boulter said it was distracting, while Harriet Dart and Francesca Jones also noticed the smell.In previous years players including Novak Djokovic and Alexander Zverev have also complained.Smoking is not permitted on site at Flushing Meadows but the smell of cannabis sometimes wafts on to court from the nearby Corona Park.It is legal to smoke it in New York for adults aged 21 and over.Victory marked Sabalenka's 16th straight win at Flushing Meadows as she bids to become the first woman since Serena Williams in 2012-2014 to complete a hat-trick of US Open singles titles.The 28-year-old showcased her trademark power from the start against Rakhimova, dropping just four points on serve in a confident opening set.Although Rakhimova fought well in the second set, Sabalenka secured the crucial break to go 5-4 up before safely serving out victory.Sabalenka served 10 aces to Rakhimova's two and did not face a single break point.She will face either American Taylor Townsend or Russian 15th seed Diana Shnaider - who beat her in the French Open quarter-finals in June - next.

schema.headline: US Open 2026 results: Aryna Sabalenka's win over Kamilla Rakhimova interrupted by cannabis smell

title: Five jailed after Lincolnshire kidnap victim jumped from window
description: Five people have been jailed after a man jumped from a first-floor window to escape kidnappers.The victim was lured to a property in Market Rasen in J
body: Five people have been jailed after a man jumped from a first-floor window to escape kidnappers.The victim was lured to a property in Market Rasen in July 2025 because of  "personal matters linked to a past relationship breakdown", Lincolnshire Police said.The force said he was "repeatedly assaulted, threatened, humiliated and tormented by his captors, while those involved filmed the abuse on their mobile phones and laughed as it unfolded".After being held overnight he was driven to a house in Lincoln, where he was caught on CCTV leaping into a tree and climbing down before running into the street and flagging down a passing police car.Armed police intercepted two of the kidnappers in a car, and the others were arrested at the house in Market Rasen.The gang were jailed at Lincoln Crown Court on 28 August.Brad'Lee Ranyard, 20, of Portland Street, Lincoln, was jailed for nine years after being convicted of kidnap and pleading guilty to false imprisonment.Jackson Nicholson, 25, of Lindsey Drive, Gainsborough, was also jailed for nine years after being convicted of kidnap and pleading guilty to false imprisonment and possessing a bladed object in public.Craig Ranyard, 42, of Barsey Walk, Horncastle, was sentenced to five years and three months in prison after pleading guilty to false imprisonment Danielle Thompson, 38, of Lime Walk, Market Rasen, was given four years and nine months after pleading guilty to false imprisonment.Nathan Gladwell, 36, of Union Street, Market Rasen, was sent to prison for three years and seven months after pleading guilty to false imprisonment.Det Con Liam Henderson said: "This was a sustained and deeply distressing ordeal in which a man was subjected to violence, threats and humiliation at the hands of people who appeared to find amusement in his suffering."The victim showed remarkable courage in seizing the opportunity to escape. The CCTV footage captures a desperate moment in which he quite literally risked everything to get away from those holding him captive."Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds, and watch the latest episode of Look North.

schema.headline: Five jailed after Lincolnshire kidnap victim jumped from window

title: US Open 2026: Naomi Osaka and Jessica Pegula on influencers causing disruption in New York
description: Lights. Camera. Quiet please...When it comes to etiquette in tennis, there are a fair few unwritten rules.Apologising after winning a point from a net
body: Lights. Camera. Quiet please...When it comes to etiquette in tennis, there are a fair few unwritten rules.Apologising after winning a point from a net cord. Honesty around line calls, double bounces and double-hits. Post-match handshakes. As for the spectators, it is common courtesy not to disturb the players during points.Around 100 influencers and content creators have been granted accreditation for the tournament in New York - double the amount from last year.Their presence has led to debate over how to balance bringing tennis to a new, different audience while respecting the game's etiquette."I definitely think it's cool to have a new demographic and I definitely think it helps grow the sport," world number four Coco Gauff said."But if you're being invited to a red carpet, you wouldn't show up in jeans."I think it's just follow the etiquette of the sport. That's all."During two-time champion Naomi Osaka's first-round match on Arthur Ashe Stadium, one group held a photo shoot in their hospitality suite while play was going on.The group turned on a portable ring light while Osaka was serving, leading to a reprimand from the umpire.When Osaka returned on Thursday, the umpire had to remind the crowd several times to be quiet."Today the umpire told everyone to be quiet more than I've ever heard an umpire tell a crowd to be quiet," Osaka said."I tell people I normally just focus on the match and the court, but there was a moment where there was people shouting and you could hear it quite clearly."I think it bothered my opponent, too."In one video, which has gone viral, a group can be seen speaking loudly as they film themselves during Osaka's first-round match on Tuesday, which led to the chair umpire calling for them to stop."I think obviously if you come to a sporting event, you have to respect the sport," Osaka said."I feel like it's common courtesy to read up on the sport, especially the etiquette."It could be a good thing for people to make the sport of tennis popular to their specific audience, but I think it has to be managed a lot better, especially in the situation like my first-round match."Overall, I think there are huge positives. You want people to continue to grow the sport. "I just think it has to be in a way that everyone knows the rules and the etiquette."Arthur Ashe is the biggest tennis stadium in the world, and matches are often accompanied by a buzz of noise from conversations around the arena.Some players love it. Some do not.Men's seventh seed Daniil Medvedev, who has had a tricky relationship with the New York crowds in the past, believes whatever brings more eyes to tennis can only be a good thing."I think the more we try to raise awareness about tennis, the better it is, the more popular the sport is," the Russian said."The more the sport grows, the better it is. I trust USTA [tournament organisers the United States Tennis Association] with what they are doing. "I think [there is] a lot more upside than downside, so go for it."American 11th seed Frances Tiafoe praised the diversity of the crowd in New York."I think the Open is great because you get all types of people that want to come and watch tennis," he said."All different walks of life, different types of people, different type of occupations. Personally, I love that."I have no problem with anybody doing anything, coming to watch the tennis."American world number three Jessica Pegula, however, said some of the behaviour had been "disrespectful"."I can appreciate the influencers coming and showcasing the US Open experience," Pegula said."But I do think that it's tough when you see videos when they're taking pictures and using the selfie lights."People are down there trying to perform. It's their career and their job. It seems a bit disrespectful."I think it's become a little too much this year. "I can appreciate one side of it, but I think when you have the other side literally interrupting matches, it gets a little tough."The US Open introduced a policy of free fan movement in 2024, meaning fans no longer have to wait to take their seats during changeovers.A year later, the tournament was expanded to 15 days. The week before the singles draw is now marketed as a 'Fan Week', showcasing the revamped mixed doubles competition and exhibition matches between players past and present.It is all part of what tournament chief executive Craig Tiley hopes will become "the tennis Disneyland".Tiley, asked about influencers being accredited in a pre-tournament news conference, said: "We need to find ways of reaching new audiences, reaching people in a way that they connect with media today."The creation of the creator credential has been a key part of that because it's enabled us to talk to people in a way that they're listening. That's been a big focus."Since the incident in Osaka's first match, there has been increased messaging on screens around the ground reminding people to "refrain from any activity that could disrupt the game, including noise levels, flash photography and ring lights".The USTA said in a statement it "is always striving to grow tennis in this country and bring new audiences into the sport"."We want all of our fans and guests to have an incredible time when they attend, but we also need to ensure they do not interfere with the action and competition on the court," it added."We are continually looking for ways to ensure fans in the stands know what is permitted and what is prohibited."

schema.headline: US Open 2026: Naomi Osaka and Jessica Pegula on influencers causing disruption in New York

title: Queen's joy at 'happy ending to a terrible story' at riot-hit library
description: The Queen visited a library rebuilt after being destroyed in a riot, telling the children she met that "you can never have too many books". Her Majest
body: The Queen visited a library rebuilt after being destroyed in a riot, telling the children she met that "you can never have too many books". Her Majesty had donated a box of books to Spellow Library in Liverpool after it was burned down in widespread unrest in the summer of 2024 following the Southport attack in which three children died. She was at the library earlier to unveil a plaque, and brought with her more books to donate.  Queen Camilla said seeing the library rise from the ashes was a "happy ending" to "such a terrible story". After unveiling the plaque, she said: "You can never have too many books. I've brought some more and it's so wonderful to see this place rise from the ashes."Congratulations to all of you who made it happen."Ahead of the plaque being unveilled, children's author Frank Cottrell-Boyce read a poem about the library.He told the Queen he had done a workshop with children to come up with a new name for the County Road site ahead of its reopening, but that the children wanted it to remain as Spellow.

schema.headline: Queen's joy at 'happy ending to a terrible story' at riot-hit library

title: Bristol woman whose XL bully killed her cousin given suspended prison sentence
description: Image source, Avon and Somerset PoliceImage caption, Kelcie Reed, 24, admitted being in charge of an XL bully that killed her teenage cousinByChloe Ha
body: Image source, Avon and Somerset PoliceImage caption, Kelcie Reed, 24, admitted being in charge of an XL bully that killed her teenage cousinByChloe HarcombeReporting fromin Bristol Crown Court and Bea SwallowBristolUpdated 7 hours agoA woman has been given a suspended prison sentence after her XL bully dog attacked and killed her cousin.Kelcie Reed, 24, of Bristol, previously admitted being in charge of a dog dangerously out control, causing the death of Morgan Dorsett.The 19-year-old, from Shrewsbury, died from neck injuries caused by the attack, which happened at Reed's flat in south Bristol in February 2025.At Bristol Crown Court, Judge Anna Richardson sentenced Reed to 18 weeks in prison, suspended for 18 months. She will also be required to undergo mental health treatment.Emergency services were called to the dog attack at a flat in Cobhorn Drive, Bishopsworth, but despite their best efforts, Morgan died from bites to her neck and face, a post-mortem examination ruled.The dog, named Prince, which belonged to Reed and her boyfriend, was sedated at the scene and later "humanely destroyed", police said.Image source, Avon and Somerset PoliceImage caption, Morgan Dorsett, 19, died after the attack in Bristol in February 2025Reed, who appeared emotional throughout the proceedings, wept in the dock as the sentence was read out.The judge told her: "Rather than putting everyone through the additional trauma of a trial, you accepted responsibility."You are someone who has over the last 18 months done what they needed to do to try and move forward. You need to continue to do that."The court heard a post-mortem examination revealed cocaine in Morgan's system, which had caused her to "act erratically"."Morgan's behaviour was unusual, and when she sat up she began to scream upon seeing Prince. That led him to barking and ultimately, he attacked her," Richardson said.The judge also noted Reed had attempted to intervene and stop the attack, suffering cuts and bruises herself, but was ultimately "unsuccessful".Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Kelcie Reed was shielded from the press as she arrived at Bristol Crown Court for sentencingIn a victim impact statement, Morgan's mother Marie Smith said the family now "lives under a shadow", with every major milestone "tainted" without her present.She told the court she struggled to sign birthday cards from the family, leaving an empty spot where her daughter's signature should be."Morgan's death has affected our family so deeply it's hard to put into words who she was and what we've lost," she said."It's something I carry with me all the time. It's impossible not to feel like something's missing. We find ourselves saying 'Morgan would've loved this' in happy moments."I don't think I'll ever be able to fully explain how much this has changed every part of our lives."Image caption, Caeila Dorsett described her older sister as a bubbly and positive personMorgan's younger sister, Caeila Dorsett, described her as a "super bubbly" and sociable person; a "built in best friend" from the day she was born."We did everything together - wore matching outfits, went to the same schools, had all the same friends, even shared a room for 16 years," she told BBC Newsbeat."She was definitely the person to take the good out of every situation and make it the centre. She was the first person I'd tell about anything exciting. "That's what I try and do now, just bring some of Morgan's positivity into my everyday life."'Loopholes' in legislationThe 19-year-old said she initially "felt sorry" for Reed having to witness the fatal attack on a family member, but that in the 18 months since the incident, she felt her cousin had "not shown any remorse or compassion".In her victim impact statement, she told the court: "We continue to live with so many unanswered questions which makes it difficult to find any sense of peace."The family say they are working alongside the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs in a bid to remove "loopholes" from current legislation around banned dog breeds. This will look at, for example, whether a dog is living with someone other than the exemption certificate holder, which can be difficult to track and enforce.PanoramaDangerous Dogs: Is the Ban Working?Det Sgt Rich Glanville from Avon and Somerset Police described the investigation as "complex and challenging", adding it was the "first of its kind" for the force."As police officers we're trained to deal with a multitude of situations, but I don't think something like this could ever be trained for," he said."It was a horrendous incident which cost someone their life, and the impact to the officers and ambulance crew that attended would be something they'll never forget."Image caption, Det Sgt Rich Glanville says Morgan's death was the first time an XL bully had killed someone in the Avon and Somerset areaGlanville said he hoped the primary takeaway from Morgan's death would be one of responsibility for dog owners, to ensure legislation is being followed and suitable precautions are considered."The dog is on the [banned breeds] list for a reason, but owners have to be responsible as well," he said."You have to look at the dog's past to try and truly understand what temperament that dog has, what training that dog has had, and whether you are a suitable person to own that type of dog."If you feel that people are not going to be safe, then you should be taking action."If you are concerned that your dog is becoming dangerous, Glanville advises contacting a vet or specially trained dog liaison officers at the force for advice.Additional reporting by Jared Evitts and Alastair McKeeGet in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Bristol

schema.headline: Bristol woman whose XL bully killed her cousin given suspended prison sentence

title: Dean says he always applied laws - but which matches did he play games in?
description: Former Premier League referee Mike Dean says he did not intend to "undermine the integrity of refereeing" after claiming that he used to play mini-gam
body: Former Premier League referee Mike Dean says he did not intend to "undermine the integrity of refereeing" after claiming that he used to play mini-games to amuse himself during matches.Dean had told Jamie Vardy's podcast that he would try to go as long as possible without blowing his whistle, or stay standing in the centre circle. "We used to say, 'we'll kick off now. Right, see how long we can go without blowing a whistle'," Dean said."I've done that a few times in the Premier League, before VAR obviously - went 20, 25 minutes without blowing a whistle."The 58-year-old has come in for considerable criticism for his comments with another former Premier League referee, Mark Halsey, telling BBC Sport that it had added extra pressure on officials today. Dean posted a statement on his Instagram story on Friday where he did not retract his claim, but sought to explain the context."Throughout my 25 years as a professional referee, I have always applied the Laws of the Game to the best of my ability," Dean wrote."My approach as a referee was always to allow the game to flow and whenever possible I preferred to apply a high threshold for contact which the players liked."However, if I saw a foul challenge that needed me to take the appropriate action I would give it from the correct position."At no stage was it my intention to question, criticise or undermine the integrity of refereeing in this country. "I have always respected the profession and the responsibility that comes with being a referee."But is there any evidence that Dean did in fact play these games?

schema.headline: Dean says he always applied laws - but which matches did he play games in?

title: Families move out of 'nightmare' new-build homes plagued by defects, damp and mould
description: Elissa and Johnnie say their "forever home" - now wrapped in scaffolding and stripped back to bare breeze block - has become a nightmare.The couple sa
body: Elissa and Johnnie say their "forever home" - now wrapped in scaffolding and stripped back to bare breeze block - has become a nightmare.The couple say they have been forced to move out of the four-bedroom property they bought 20 months ago.An independent inspector, known as a "snagger", made a report identifying about 150 faults - including wonky walls, bowing windows and a poorly fitted kitchen.Elissa, who has a long‑term health condition, says the stress has led to hospital visits. The couple are now in a rental home for the second time this year, while repairs are carried out.Elissa is one of dozens of people from across the UK who have got in touch with BBC Your Voice about problems with new-build properties.We have heard accounts from homeowners who bought outright, often with a mortgage, as well as those who purchased through shared-ownership schemes. Renters in brand-new flats and people who have moved into new social housing also got in touch. Everyone said they had felt stressed and desperate.One new owner in Somerset told us she had found black mould throughout her property; a tenant in London said ceilings had collapsed in her apartment block; while a third resident in Essex described how his social housing property had been full of mould and damp when he moved in.Their stories come as the number of complaints to the New Homes Ombudsman Service (NHOS) has more than tripled in a year, according to its latest annual report.The UK-wide service received just over 1,800 complaints in 2025-26, up from fewer than 600 the previous year. Defects and snagging were the most common issues raised.The ombudsman says the increase partly reflects more homeowners being eligible to use the service, as well as greater awareness of it.The voluntary NHOS was set up by big stakeholders in the building industry, and although registrations increased by 26% in the past financial year, still about a third of all new homes sit outside the scheme - including Elissa and Johnnie's.The service can intervene when developers are "unable or unwilling to fix" problems, but it only covers new properties purchased outright - not those bought under shared-ownership.It is a situation that MPs and chief ombudsman, Nigel Cates, say urgently needs to change.Responding to those concerns, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told us the government planned to set-up a mandatory ombudsman as soon as parliamentary time allowed, adding that homes should be "safe" and "built to last".In 2022, the Conservative government committed to establishing such a service as part of the Building Safety Act, aimed at strengthening safety and regulatory standards in light of the Grenfell Tower tragedy.Elissa and Johnnie moved in to their home in North Lincolnshire just before Christmas 2024. After the initial excitement, they soon started to find defects and decided to hire the snagger.They moved out for the first time in the new year, while Stonebridge Homes agreed to send in a contractor to carry out remedial work."It was absolutely shocking. I had to stand there and allow this guy to do work on my house, and he made it worse!" says Johnnie.An independent surveyor's report for Stonebridge Homes, seen by the BBC, described the mortar work as "low standard" that would make "cracking more likely".It also suggested the home's outer walls had an "inward lean" with a deviation of up to 50mm. Structural warranty providers say the maximum should be 8mm over a three-metre stretch.The couple say they have spent hundreds of hours dealing with the problems. Elissa says she has gone to hospital several times with chest pains that medics have attributed to "stress"."We are strong people, but we are really struggling," she says.In a statement, Stonebridge Homes apologised to the couple and said it was in discussion with them about the construction of their home. It said it had arranged "alternative accommodation and all associated relocation costs" while work is carried out.The developer has also offered to buy the home back from Elissa and Johnnie, but the couple say they would end up about £100,000 out of pocket, having spent thousands on renovating, refurbishing and landscaping - as well as solicitors fees and Stamp Duty.Other residents on the 48-home development have also reported problems. The BBC understands at least one further family has had to move out for renovation works.Elissa and Johnnie believe quality control during the build was lacking and more "stringent legislation" is needed so builders know "they can't build more rubbish homes".Elissa says a senior Stonebridge employee told her they were under "pressure" to increase output and sometimes that compromised quality.We asked Stonebridge Homes about this, along with all the points of criticism raised above, but the company did not provide specific answers.It told the BBC that customer service was one of its top priorities as well as access to "clear, transparent processes for raising concerns and seeking independent resolution where required".One of the biggest issues for homebuyers, says ombudsman Cates, is not the defects they find, but the way they feel treated by developers when they complain."For most people, this is the biggest purchase they'll ever make. So, when something goes wrong, they need the developer to be on it straight away, take them seriously, really value them, understand them and put it right," he tells us.New homes are inspected several times during construction by either local council building inspectors or a registered building control approver, to make sure they meet legal, national building regulations. Most developers also use insurance providers, who carry out their own checks and offer 10-year warranties.The government has set itself a target of building 1.5 million homes in England by 2029. As housebuilding speeds up, the industry could be "setting itself up for a huge fail", says John Cooper, director of snagging company New Home Quality Control.His inspectors frequently find breaches of building regulations, he tells us, including insulation, brickwork and carpentry problems. "We see some horrors," he says, adding that current checks on new homes before handover are insufficient.A panel of experts recently told MPs on the Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee that parts of the building industry are like the "wild west" and there needs to be a more robust, uniform system.Cates, who sat on the panel, told MPs that residents not covered by NHOS faced a "patchwork of [building] codes" not designed to help homeowners.He tells the BBC there is "a big difference between having a code, and standards very specifically tailored to modern home sales, and the issues coming with that"."It's critical for the whole industry... that everyone has the same protections, access to an ombudsman service and an impartial investigation," he adds.The body representing big developers, the Home Builders Federation, says it supports a statutory ombudsman, so all new-build buyers are covered, but wants the government to reduce what it describes as the "regulatory burden", including extra taxes and policy costs, which have rendered many potential sites, and businesses, "no longer viable".For Jess and her partner Darryl, NHOS could not help as it does not cover shared-ownership homes. The couple found black mould in their house 10 days after moving in.The mother of three from Somerset told BBC Your Voice they put all their savings into the home. "We feel like we're living in a nightmare".L&G told the BBC its priority was that The Fold's residents were "safe, supported and kept informed".The complex had already been built - and approved by building control - before L&G "took it on", it said. Independent fire safety experts, including the London Fire Brigade and the Building Safety Regulator (BSR), had confirmed the buildings were safe while investigative work was being carried out, it added, with each apartment compensated with £8,500 on average.A London Fire Brigade spokesperson said it had carried out a fire safety inspection under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005, and while some defects were identified, formal action was not considered necessary. It added that its remit under the legislation covers communal areas including the front door of a property.The BSR told us it would not describe its involvement as providing general assurance that the building was safe, noting that the duty holder normally retains responsibility. It said its role was to assess compliance with the Building Safety Act 2022.In Essex, Luke Weaver got in touch with BBC Your Voice because his new home had damp and mould that he believed was making his two-year-old son ill.However, his case is different from others because, as a social housing tenant, he was able to obtain support from an ombudsman service, separate from NHOS, which social-housing providers must join.The Housing Ombudsman covers social housing in England and private landlords can sign up voluntarily. But this ombudsman can only deal with housing providers, not developers.Other parts of the UK have similar ombudsmen schemes.A surveyor working for Luke's housing association, Clarion, found wet insulation inside a wall and further inspections identified elevated moisture levels.The Housing Ombudsman found Clarion had not handled the damp, mould and snagging issues appropriately even though the builder, Dandara, would still have been responsible during the defect period.Clarion apologised to Luke and said it was complying with the ombudsman's orders, including paying him £1,150 in compensation and arranging a further inspection of his home.Dandara said it took reports of damp and mould seriously and was "committed to working with Clarion and the resident" to address any concerns.It said an End of Defects inspection in August found a small number of minor items, due for completion this month, and added it had requested the Housing Ombudsman's conclusions from Clarion.Luke says the findings have left him feeling "vindicated" and relieved. But he says the situation remains unresolved, with the source of the damp still to be identified and any remedial work yet to be carried out. He does not believe he would have received the same support without the ombudsman.Additional reporting by Kris Bramwell

schema.headline: Families move out of 'nightmare' new-build homes plagued by defects, damp and mould

title: Jude Bellingham: England midfielder looks ready to show full potential at Real Madrid
description: Jude Bellingham has started the new season looking like a player with something to prove.The 23-year-old's two goals and three assists have helped Rea
body: Jude Bellingham has started the new season looking like a player with something to prove.The 23-year-old's two goals and three assists have helped Real Madrid to an impressive start under new boss Jose Mourinho, with three wins from as many games.Bellingham's performances, and the freedom he has been given in his new role, has attracted a lot of attention.By playing higher up the pitch, he looks more free, more influential and closer to the role in which he first made such an impact at the Bernabeu in his debut 2023-24 season, where he scored 23 goals as his side won La Liga and the Champions League.Bellingham's last two campaigns were less consistent, with his displays and attacking influence affected not only by a deeper role, but by recurring injuries. He had a long-standing shoulder problem that required surgery in 2025 and a hamstring issue that kept him out for 10 matches in 2026.Now, however, he appears to be at peak fitness, ready to build on his impressive World Cup form for England and showcase the full extent of his talent.Since returning this summer to take charge of the club for a second spell, Mourinho has made an important adjustment in reducing the defensive workload that previously meant Bellingham had to cover huge areas of the pitch."We've organised the team differently," he said after Real Madrid's 4-0 La Liga win over Malaga."Bellingham sometimes defended like a second left-back last season. I told him I do not want to see that anymore. I made a deal with him."The Portuguese manager has used Bellingham primarily as a number 10 in a 4-2-3-1 system, operating behind French striker Kylian Mbappe and with the freedom to move across the attacking line.That gives the England midfielder a clearer role. Rather than constantly moving between midfield, defence and attack, he can spend more time in the areas where he is most dangerous."For me, this is his position, with his connection with the forwards, he can score goals," added Mourinho."He has to play close to the goal. Playing at number six or number eight, we're losing his closeness to the goal. I like this Jude."It has meant Bellingham can receive the ball between the lines, carry it forward, combine with the forwards and make late runs into the penalty area.Just as importantly, he is being given greater freedom to decide when to move.Bellingham has explained the difference himself in an interview with Real Madrid TV."I feel more free to decide when to drop back, when to stay up or when to get into the box," he said. "I think this is the best position for me."Mourinho still expects him to press and recover possession, but the difference is where that work begins. Instead of dropping deep towards his own penalty area, Bellingham can now use his energy to press opponents higher up the pitch.When Madrid win the ball, he is already closer to the forwards. That allows him to connect midfield with attack and provide another player who can combine with Mbappe and Vinicius Jr.It also explains why Mourinho has been keen to stress Madrid's attacking players must work together rather than operate as individuals."The team dynamic is about 11, not 2+9," he said.The midfielder also described working with Mourinho as a "dream", having previously only met the former Chelsea, Manchester United and Tottenham manager once before his appointment.There is clearly an early understanding and respect between the two.Mourinho has repeatedly spoken about Bellingham's importance to his plans, describing him as a "unique and super important player" with qualities that include physical, mental and tactical. He also suggested Bellingham should be one of the players in the running for the Ballon d'Or."He is a unique kind of player and extremely important for the team," said Mourinho."His mental strength, tactical ability, the way he recovers the ball, the way he pressures, the way he plays up front, I am very happy."For Mourinho, that versatility is part of what makes Bellingham so valuable. He can press, recover possession, score, contribute in the air and drive the team forward.The Real boss has also pointed to Thomas Tuchel's use of Bellingham at the World Cup as an example of how to get the best out of him.Bellingham was one of England's standout players, finishing with seven goals and an assist in his eight appearances, and his attacking qualities were allowed to flourish.That experience also appears to have given the player a confidence boost, particularly as he rejoined Madrid later than most of his team-mates and had less time to prepare for the new campaign. Although Real's three league wins - scoring 10 goals and conceding two - are only a small sample, and the demands will increase as the season progresses amid Champions League football, the early signs are very positive.For Bellingham, whose huge strength has always been his ability to affect almost every part of a game, Mourinho's system has given him more control over where that influence is used.After a difficult couple of seasons following the high standards he set in his first year, the England midfielder is enjoying his football again."I'm having a lot of fun, I'm really enjoying my football, and that's why I'm performing well," he told club media.If he continues in this vein with Mourinho's continued support, it could turn out to be his best season yet.

schema.headline: Jude Bellingham: England midfielder looks ready to show full potential at Real Madrid
